“No.” Calder closed the folder. “The human word is should. But courts require evidence, procedure, and an opportunity for the other side to answer. We cannot replace one failure with another, even when the answer feels obvious.”

I understood. I hated that I understood.

“Will they tell him?” I asked.

“They will notify the prison that a review is being sought. He may hear before the newspapers do.”

I pictured Jonah as I had last seen him, though the memory was old and incomplete: the stillness of his shoulders, the controlled way he held his hands, the look of a man trying not to hope because hope had become another thing authorities could take away.

“How long?”

Calder did not pretend to know. “Months. Possibly longer.”

“He has already given them eleven years.”

“Yes.”

The word sat between us. No explanation could enter it.

That evening I walked alone to the end of the harbour. The island had resumed its ordinary noises: gulls, ropes knocking against masts, a delivery van reversing somewhere behind the cottages. Blackwater stood on the cliff, fenced now with temporary barriers and warning signs. In daylight, it looked less like a trap than a large damaged house.

That was the danger of daylight. It made ruin appear manageable.

I took Jonah’s name from my notebook and wrote beneath it: Conviction under review. Statement submitted. Evidence transferred.

Then I added: Eleven years cannot be transferred.

I closed the book.

The law might clear Jonah Rusk. It might name Simon Kreel as the architect of a chain of crimes, distinguish the crimes he had committed from those he had concealed, and establish facts where Blackwater had preserved only rumours. It might put Jonah in a courtroom and return his name to him in a judgment written by people who had never watched the years pass through a prison window.

None of that would give him back the years.

None of it would remove my voice from the first conviction.

I had wanted evidence to be a door. I had imagined that once it opened, we would all pass through and stand somewhere clean. But evidence was not absolution. It was only the light by which responsibility could be seen.

Behind me, the harbour master rang the bell for the evening ferry. Across the water, Blackwater’s broken observatory caught the last strip of sun. For an instant, the shattered glass shone like stars.

Then the light moved, and the house became what it had always been: timber, stone, metal, and the choices of the people who entered it.

I turned toward the town, carrying the notebook in my uninjured hand.

The house was open now.

What came next would have to be faced in the light.

chapters.name: Into the Light
chapters.content:
On the morning I was due to leave Blackwater Island, I went back to the observatory.

I did not tell Celia. Orr was at the schoolhouse, writing in the careful hand that refused to make certainty out of grief. Agnes had gone to her cottage near the harbour, where a window faced away from the house. The police had finished their first examination but had not released the estate. A barrier stood across the path, and a laminated notice warned the curious that entry was prohibited.

I showed my pass to the constable at the gate.

“Alone?” he asked.

“That is the intention.”

He looked at my splint, my bruised face, and the way I held my ribs when I climbed. “If the intention changes, shout.”

“I’ll try to keep it simple.”

The observatory rose above the house with its broken frame open to the sky. In the night it had been a theatre of black glass and moving shadows. In daylight it looked wounded rather than supernatural. Rain had dried in pale tracks on the remaining panes. The outer bridge had been locked in place with temporary braces. Police tape crossed the threshold, fluttering in the wind like a tired flag.

I ducked beneath it.

The first thing daylight did was return the room to its measurements.

The steel door was not a sealed mystery. It was a door with a warped lower hinge, a deadbolt scarred by repeated use, and a narrow channel beneath the plate where a cord could once have passed. The keyhole was stamped with the compass rose, not because the symbol belonged to anything occult but because Elias Vale had liked to turn practical hardware into a signature.

The windows were not impossible windows. They were framed panels with concealed catches and a system of locking bars that had failed under fire and storm. The brass meridian circle was not an instrument that had reached out to kill a man. It was a piece of engineered apparatus, altered by someone who understood where a spring could be hidden and how far a needle would travel.

The room still contained the astronomical table, though the table had been split and strapped to a wooden pallet. The needle housing sat inside a clear evidence box. A label gave it a number. Another label recorded the minute blood trace recovered from the meridian circle. A third identified the aconitine residue.

Numbers had replaced dread.

I stood just inside the door and tried to remember the moment I had first seen Vale dead. The key in his hand. The papers scattered near his chair. The rain striking the glass. My mind had wanted the room to be impossible because impossibility seemed cleaner than murder. If no one could have entered, then perhaps no one had truly chosen to do what had been done.

But a locked room was not a moral category. It did not make a death pure. It only described the limits someone had arranged around it.

I crossed to the star map. The map had been removed after the counterweight nearly crushed me, leaving a rectangle of dustless wall and a forest of exposed gears. Some had melted at their edges. Others were black with smoke. A fine chain hung slack between two wheels. One of the counterweights had been tagged and secured, but its weight was still visible through the open housing: a dark block of iron, no larger than a suitcase, suspended above the drop shaft.

The constable had been right to ask me to shout.

I kept my distance from the machinery and looked instead at the wall behind it. There were seams everywhere now. A vertical line where a panel had been fitted. A circle around the compass rose. A narrow rectangle beneath the speaking-tube mouth. While the house had been operating around us, those lines had vanished into shadow, polish, and expectation. In daylight they declared themselves.

The house had not lied by changing shape.

It had lied by showing only the shape a person was prepared to notice.

Kreel had known that. He had known which corridor could be made to seem occupied by a reflection, which voice could travel farther than a body, which paper could be moved without opening the case, which mechanism could turn a witness toward the wrong door. He had understood that an alibi did not need to be true if it was witnessed by the architecture.

The Wren case had depended on the same weakness.

I took my notebook from my coat. The right hand could not manage the clasp properly, so I held the book against my hip and worked it open with my left. On a clean page I wrote:

The observatory was not locked because the murderer was absent.

It was locked because the victim was persuaded to enter it alone.

The poison had done the rest.

I paused, then added:

The key proved only that Vale held the key.

It did not prove that he understood the room.

That had been the center of the case, and yet it was not the center of the crime. We had spent days asking how a killer could enter a sealed observatory, when the more important question was why Vale had believed the room would protect him. The answer lay in the threats, the folder, the buried records, and his fear of the people who knew what Blackwater had concealed.

He had gone to the observatory because he thought privacy was safety.

Kreel had built the trap years before Vale walked into it.

A gust came through the open frame, carrying the smell of salt and wet stone. Somewhere below, a loose shutter struck the house in an irregular rhythm. I looked down through the broken edge of the floor toward the gallery. The vertical shaft behind the compass rose dropped through darkness, though the police had fixed a work light beside it. The beam showed the ladder, the brackets, the scraped paint where I had climbed, and nothing mysterious at all.

Nothing mysterious. Everything deliberate.

I thought of Gabriel Rusk beneath the western retaining wall. Of Livia, whose last certainty had been reduced to a letter and the memory of people who had failed to stop her disappearance. Of Adrian, whose death had been dressed in a story about his sister. Of Vale, who had finally decided to tell the truth and had trusted the house he had inherited with his life.

The buried chamber had been called the drowned room, as if water had made it secret. But water did not keep a secret. People did. They built a wall. They altered a plan. They sealed a culvert. They taught a house to carry voices away from the person who had spoken them.

The true locked room was not the observatory.

It was the conspiracy built around the buried chamber and the dead whose stories had been sealed beneath the house.

Its door had been made from fear, loyalty, money, and the ordinary wish to avoid knowing what knowledge would demand. Its lock was not steel. It was the agreement, repeated over decades, that reputation mattered more than a vanished man, that a frightened woman could be dismissed, that a convenient plan was as good as a verified fact.

I had been part of another version of that lock.

The thought did not arrive as a revelation. It had been waiting for me since the Wren papers were opened in the schoolhouse. I had mistaken an architectural possibility for an established route. I had accepted authority where I should have tested material fact. I had given the jury a coherent story in the place of a complete chain of evidence.

Kreel had engineered the conditions. He had exploited the error. But he had not held my hand while I spoke.

The distinction mattered in court. It did not absolve me.

I closed the notebook and stood for a while beneath the broken compass rose. The symbol had once seemed to point toward a hidden answer. Now it pointed in four ordinary directions, each leading to a different part of the house, each dependent on a human hand to move a latch or release a weight.

A compass did not choose a destination.

Neither did evidence.

When I left the observatory, the constable was waiting by the barrier. He looked past me into the room.

“Any trouble?”

“Only the usual kind.”

He did not smile. “Calder wants you at the harbour office before the ferry.”

The harbour office was warmer than the observatory and smelled of coffee, damp uniforms, and the sea. Detective Inspector Ruth Calder sat at a desk beneath a window where sunlight made the dust visible. Her folder was thicker than it had been four days earlier. The evidence had acquired reports, signatures, times, and cross-references. The case was becoming a structure other people would have to enter.

She stood when I came in, then thought better of offering me a chair and pointed instead to the one nearest the stove.

“How is the wrist?”

“Still attached.”

“Your standards remain low.”

“They’re improving.”

She gave me the briefest smile. Then she placed a form on the desk.

“The Crown will want your evidence,” she said. “Not only about Kreel’s admissions and the observatory. The Wren material. The chain by which the plans reached the investigation. What you were told. What you assumed. What you failed to check.”

“I know.”

“You may be questioned by the prosecution. The defence will question you more severely.”

“I know that too.”

Calder studied me. “Do you?”

The sunlight had moved across the floor between us. Outside, a gull landed on the office roof and scraped its feet against the metal.

“I know that saying I was deceived will not be enough,” I said. “It will be true, but it won’t be enough. I gave the testimony. I described the route as if possibility were proof. Jonah Rusk lost eleven years because I was certain in the wrong direction.”

“You were not the only person involved.”

“No. But I was one of them.”

Calder slid the form toward me. “Will you testify?”

The question had a simple shape. It did not have a simple answer. Testifying meant entering a courtroom where Kreel’s counsel could take apart every conclusion I had made, including the conclusions that now condemned Kreel. It meant allowing strangers to hear how confidently I had spoken about Jonah. It meant that a successful review would carry my name in its history, not as the sole cause but not as an incidental one either.

For a moment I wanted the ferry to leave without me. I wanted to go somewhere anonymous, where Blackwater could become a story told by people who had never stood in its machinery and watched a choice turn into a fact.

Then I thought of Jonah receiving notice in a prison office. I thought of hope being handed to him by the same system that had taken it away. If I asked him to trust a review, I could not refuse the part of it that required my voice.

“Yes,” I said.

Calder nodded once. She did not congratulate me.

“I will testify,” I said. “About Kreel. About the evidence. About what I got wrong.”

“That is what the form says.”

“I want it written that way.”

“It will be.”

I signed with my left hand. The letters were uneven, but they were mine.

When I stepped outside, the ferry was sounding its first warning from the quay. Celia stood near the gangway with Orr. He carried a case of his papers and a bundle of copied notes. She had one small bag and the legal packet concerning the public trust. Neither looked toward the cliff.

Agnes was not there. She had said goodbye at the cottage, and I had not asked her to repeat it at the harbour. Some departures needed to be allowed to remain complete.

Orr saw the form in my hand. “Calder?”

“Testimony.”

He nodded. “Good.”

“Good is a large word.”

“Then use a smaller one.”

I looked across the water. Blackwater House stood above the island, fenced and scarred, its observatory open to the morning. The building no longer appeared to be waiting for someone to solve it. It was waiting for people to stop mistaking its silence for innocence.

“Necessary,” I said.

The ferry bell rang again.

I put the notebook into my coat and walked toward the gangway with my damaged wrist held close and the signed statement in my other hand. Behind me, the island kept the house. Ahead of me lay the courts, the review, the questions, and the long work of separating what had happened from what I had once believed.

Daylight did not make the truth beautiful.

It made it visible.

That would have to be enough.
